title: Large-Scale Notification Dispatch with Bundle Treatments and Multi-Outcome Uplift Optimization
one_liner: Choose one notification plan per user by estimating the extra effect of each timing-and-style bundle, then solve a constrained assignment problem that respects global send limits and device quotas.
lead: A large app does not merely decide whether to send a notification. It must decide when to send it, how to present it, how many total notifications the platform can afford to send, and how many each device vendor will tolerate before throttling or user fatigue becomes a problem. The paper treats each timing-and-style choice as a bundle treatment, estimates the incremental change each bundle causes on several outcomes, and then separates prediction from action. BUOPLR first learns small bundle-level uplift values, then solves a large constrained assignment problem with a pruned Lagrangian method so the final policy can raise Daily Active Users without violating platform rules.

problem.h2: Why notification dispatch becomes an optimization problem
paras: For one user, sending a notification can increase app opens, but it can also raise dismissals, opt-outs, or wasted impressions. For a platform with more than 100 million daily users, the decision space grows quickly because each user may receive several timing choices and several presentation styles. Picking the best action therefore means comparing many bundles, not just send versus do not send.

A direct rule such as "send the bundle with the highest predicted click rate" fails because the platform has shared limits. There may be a daily notification budget, vendor-specific quota rules, and several business outcomes that matter at once. The right action for one user depends on what the system is already sending to everyone else, because every extra send consumes part of a limited global resource.

callout.html: Estimate the extra effect of each bundle on several outcomes, then pick user-level actions with a separate constrained solver because prediction alone cannot enforce shared platform limits.

panels.caption: BUOPLR separates estimation from the final assignment step.

panels.title: 5. Feasible lift at scale
panels.caption: The system raises engagement while staying inside dispatch constraints.

steps.text: Treat each timing-and-style combination as one action, because the effect of timing depends on presentation and vice versa.
Predict the incremental change each bundle causes on several outcomes for each user, because the policy must trade one outcome against others.
Restrict the action set per user to a smaller candidate list, because most bundles are clearly poor and only add solver cost.
Attach prices to the global constraints and score each remaining bundle with those penalties, because this turns a hard coupled problem into many easier user-level choices.
Send the chosen bundles only after the total assignment satisfies budget and quota rules.

paras: The paper changes notification dispatch from a ranking problem into a constrained allocation problem. It also changes the treatment definition: instead of modeling timing and style separately, it models the joint bundle because those choices interact.

hidden.name: incremental value per bundle under shared constraints
paras: The deciding quantity is not the predicted probability that a user opens the app after a notification. It is the uplift, meaning the extra change caused by sending one bundle instead of the baseline. This matters because a user who would open the app anyway should not consume scarce notification budget unless the bundle changes behavior enough to justify the cost.

That uplift must also be interpreted together with constraint shadow prices, which are the effective costs of spending one more unit of a limited resource. A bundle with positive uplift can still be a bad final choice if it consumes too much of a scarce vendor quota. BUOPLR estimates bundle-level uplift first, then combines it with these learned costs during assignment.

reads.html: The system needs to know how much a bundle changes behavior beyond what would have happened anyway, then subtract the cost of using scarce sending capacity.
BUOPLR estimates bundle-level multi-outcome uplift and then combines those estimates with Lagrange multipliers, which are learned penalty values for violating global dispatch constraints.

paras: The first stage exists because the signal is small. A notification usually changes behavior only a little, so the model has to borrow structure across related bundles and related outcomes instead of learning every effect in isolation. Sharing information across timing choices and presentation styles reduces variance in the estimated uplift because a rare bundle can still benefit from patterns seen in similar bundles.

The second stage exists because the assignment is globally coupled. If the system tried to learn the full dispatch policy end to end, it would need to reason over millions of linked choices at once. BUOPLR instead turns each constraint into a penalty term. When those penalty values are set well, each user can be scored independently by "uplift minus resource cost," and the separate choices add up to a feasible global solution because the penalties push the policy away from overusing scarce resources.

Pruning matters because the raw action space is large. Removing obviously weak bundles lowers solver cost and reduces the chance that estimation noise on a poor action changes the final decision. The result is a practical pipeline: estimate subtle causal effects, keep only plausible actions, then solve the constrained allocation with penalties that summarize the system-wide trade-offs.

stages.s: learn multi-outcome uplift for each bundle
attach penalty values for budget and vendor quotas
pick the best feasible bundle per user

math.words: Choose the bundle whose estimated gain minus the weighted cost of consumed constraints is largest, while allowing a no-send option.
math.equation: score(user, bundle) = uplift_DAU - lambda_budget * budget_use - sum_v mu_v * quota_use_v

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose a noon banner for one user has estimated DAU uplift 0.08.
It consumes 1 unit of global budget and 1 unit of a tight vendor quota.
If the current budget penalty is 0.01 and the vendor penalty is 0.05, the score is 0.08 - 0.01 - 0.05 = 0.02.
A quiet evening card with uplift 0.06 and only the budget cost would score 0.06 - 0.01 = 0.05.
The second bundle wins even though its raw uplift is smaller, because the first bundle spends scarcer capacity.

math.note: The penalties summarize the global trade-off, so each user-level choice reflects system-wide scarcity.

charts.title: Simple ranking policy
charts.note: A local ranking policy can pick attractive bundles for many users, but it spends shared capacity without pricing scarcity into the decision.

charts.title: BUOPLR
charts.note: BUOPLR keeps strong per-user choices while respecting budgets, because the assignment stage converts global constraints into explicit per-bundle costs.

items.b: Uplift estimates can be too noisy.
items.html: If the estimated extra effect per bundle is mostly noise, the solver will optimize unreliable scores because the second stage trusts the first stage's ranking.

items.b: Pruning can remove the real winner.
items.html: A bundle that looks weak under a coarse filter may become the best choice after quota costs are counted, so over-aggressive pruning can cap the final policy.

items.b: Penalty values can converge to the wrong scarcity level.
items.html: If the Lagrangian update does not match the true platform bottlenecks, the final assignment may underuse budget or keep violating a quota because the learned costs are miscalibrated.

The method works best when bundle-level causal estimates are stable, the candidate pruning step keeps all serious options, and the penalty updates are monitored against actual budget and vendor usage.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Create a synthetic notification simulator with four bundle treatments per user, one no-send option, a global send budget, and two vendor quotas. Generate user-level uplift values for DAU and one negative outcome such as opt-out risk.

Train a small bundle-uplift predictor, prune to the top few bundles per user, and solve the assignment with Lagrangian penalties. Compare against a policy that chooses the largest predicted uplift independently for each user. The demo should show that the independent policy breaks shared limits, while the penalty-based assignment preserves most of the lift because it prices scarce resources directly into the decision.
demo.closing: A convincing demo should show high feasible_lift together with zero budget and quota violations.
